title: Slip knot
subtitle: The adjustable loop that starts almost every piece
excerpt: The slip knot is the first loop you put on the hook. It is a sliding knot that snugs up around the hook and undoes again if you change your mind. Nearly every chain, every foundation, and every motif begins here.
sourceNotes: Reconstructed in our own words from Thérèse de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), Chapter 9 (Crochet Work), the opening passage on starting a chain (the loop placed on the hook before the first chain). Public domain via Project Gutenberg.

glossaryTerms.definition: A sliding knot tied around the hook to make the first loop. It tightens when you pull the working yarn and loosens when you pull the tail, so it can be adjusted or undone before you commit.
The strand running from the ball that feeds into each stitch. The other short end left after the knot is the tail.
The short cut end of yarn left over after the slip knot, usually about 10 cm. It gets woven in at the end.

Lay the yarn across your palm with the tail hanging down about 10 cm.
Make a loop by crossing the working yarn over the tail, so the two strands form a circle.
Reach through the loop and draw a fold of the working yarn back through it, making a second loop.
Slide that second loop onto the hook and pull both ends gently to snug it up.
Check the fit. The loop should sit close to the hook but still slide. If it grips too tightly, ease it open; if it is loose and floppy, pull the working yarn to draw it in.

The slip knot starts a foundation chain, which in turn starts most flat and in-the-round projects. It is also the loop you put back on the hook when you join a new colour or a new ball partway through a piece. Any time a pattern says to begin, this is usually the first move.

Some crocheters skip the knot entirely and simply loop the yarn over the hook, holding the tail to keep it from sliding off; this leaves a slightly neater start but takes more control. For working in the round, the magic ring replaces the slip knot with an adjustable centre loop that closes tight. The slip knot is the plainest and most forgiving of these starts, which is why it is the one to learn first.
Difficulty: beginner. This is the very first thing most people learn, and it takes only a few tries for the hands to remember.
